newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's army calls for action against Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's army calls for action against Islamists.

text.p: Turkey's powerful military launched the latest round in its feud with the Islamist-led government on Wednesday with a call on citizens to rise up against the danger of Moslem activism.

"It is the main duty of every secularist and democratic citizen who loves his country...not to stand neutral and to act against the increasing reactionary threat," General Fevzi Turkeri told reporters at a briefing on resurgent Islamism.

The secularist army and Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party have been engaged in a fierce battle since February when a military-dominated security council ordered a crackdown on religious activity in public life.

The row has brought Erbakan's 11-month-old coalition with conservatives to breaking point. On Wednesday the junior coalition partner Tansu Ciller said a change of government was expected within days to resolve the crisis.
"A change of government is expected in the coming days," Ciller told deputies from her True Path Party (DYP) in parliament.

However, Turkish law requires the president and later parliament to approve any change in government, and it remains uncertain the government, now lacking a clear majority, could see through any such change.
The military accuses Erbakan, Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, of threatening the secular order by promoting Islamic groups, among which they said were militant elements.
"Within the reactionary elements, it is seen that there are as many as 30 groups which are radical who will most probably turn to terrorist activities," Turkeri said.
He also attacked Erbakan for hosting a meal for leaders of Turkey's tarikats, or religious sects, during the Moslem holy month of Ramadan. The tarikats are technically illegal but largely tolerated.

"The arrival at the prime minister's residence of religious sect leaders known for their verbal and active opposition to secularism...gave a message to these people that they were respected at the level of the state and their activities were tolerated," Turkeri said.

A string of pro-Islamist government proposals in February prompted the demands from the security council for an anti-Islamist crackdown, including restrictions on the role of religious schools and the closing of unofficial Koran courses.
Erbakan has stalled on implementing the council's demands and announced on June 1 that his coalition with conservatives would seek early elections to resolve the row.
The two parties did not set a date for elections, which must be approved by parliament, but a senior member of Erbakan's party said on Wednesday polls were expected to take place in October.
At Wednesday's briefing, the military said Iran was playing a role in the spread of Islamist activism in Turkey.
"Iran is providing every kind of support to build a regime in Turkey based on the principles of Sharia (Moslem holy law)," Turkeri said.

Erbakan has sought to foster links with Iran since coming to power last June, but the secularist establishment has continued to protest at what it sees as Iranian support for separatist Kurdish rebels.
The military last week said Iran was sponsoring Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas engaged in an armed struggle with the security forces for self rule in southeast Turkey.

More than 10,000 Turkish troops are involved in a four-week-old operation against the guerrillas in northern Iraq. The incursion has drawn strong criticism from NATO-member Turkey's western allies and Middle Eastern countries.
